en: The Sūtra on the Ritual Manual of the Noble Treasure God, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master of the Transmission of the Teaching, the Subject Fǎtiān, in accordance with the Imperial Decree.

I take refuge in all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. I prostrate to the Lord of the Treasure (Kuberavaiśravaṇa), who, according to the Dharma, brings joy to the deities of the treasure and fulfills all the aims of seekers.
Now I shall explain the extensive ritual manual and the rules for the homa of the Lord of the Treasure.
If one who maintains this recitation must single-mindedly take refuge in the Triple Gem and first receive empowerment,
they should practice compassion and patience for the sake of all sentient beings.
One should practice with deep faith according to the Dharma as it has been taught.
One who possesses these qualities may perform the ritual procedures for recitation.
Before performing this rite, one should first sit down comfortably and thoroughly purify one's body and mind.
One should contemplate a pure site suitable for establishing the halls and pavilions of the noble and holy ones:
namely, the banks of rivers, within groves and gardens, inside mountain ravines,
at places where noble sages have practiced walking meditation, and at sites bearing the traces of the holy ones.
A place free from thieves, where the three evils do not arise, a pure land;
a single location that is exceptionally sublime,
as well as a clean ground devoid of snakes, insects, mosquitoes, and gadflies.
Remove the tiles and stones.
Take clean earth from the riverbank to fill [the area] and level it.
Use the five kinds of pure water.
Recite the Heart Mantra and the Outer Heart Mantra eight hundred times;
empower the water and sprinkle it upon that ground.
First, recite the mantra as you arise.
When one has obtained auspicious omens,
one should then face either east, west, or north at that location.
Construct a vast, sublime, and noble hall for the sages.
Furthermore, use five kinds of pure water to purify oneself;
empower this water by reciting the mantra eight thousand times.
One should give alms to all sentient beings, including hungry ghosts and others;
yet one must personally maintain a sincere vow of purity and observe the precepts,
bathing three times each day.
Furthermore, at the three times of day, one changes into fresh,
clean robes and practices while contemplating the three sublime liberations in one's mind.
Thus one proceeds.
In the evening, enter this ritual arena and perform the recitation until the time of the morning meal.
When the sun has half-risen, conclude the recitation.
Thereafter, take a small amount of pure earth and place it into pure water.
Having washed the upper part of the body,
one should then remain silent, facing east,
or facing west, or facing north.
Sitting upright, wash the lower part of the body.
Then, separately take pure earth mixed with water and rinse the mouth three times while reciting the Holy Invincible Mantra (*Aparājita-mantra*).
Rubbing the crown of the head with one's hand, perform the empowerment three times;
thus, one immediately attains protection for oneself.
Then, prostrate to the noble deities and recite either the heart mantra or the outer heart mantra.
Consecrate the scented water three times and sprinkle it within the Hall of the Worthies and Sages; then,
present twenty kinds of offerings.
Form the samādhi-mudrā to create the vajra-wall;
form the vajra-kīla-mudrā to create the vajra-net.
Then, place the palms of both hands flat against each other.
Place the two middle fingers side by side;
bend the third joints of the two ring fingers;
and place the two index fingers against the backs of those ring fingers.
Place the two thumbs alongside the two index fingers;
let the two little fingers be like vajra needles.
This is the fundamental mudrā of the deity Ratnapāṇi.
When this mudrā is bound at the center, the deity Ratnagarbha shall appear.
Then, recite the root mantra:
*Namo ratnatrayāya, namo maṇibhadrāya mahāyakṣasenāpataye, oṃ jaṃ jvala ra re ya svāhā*. Then, recite the heart mantra.
*Ratnapālanatejajvalanaya svāhā*. Then, recite the Outer Heart Mantra.
*Ratnapālanatejajvalanamukhe nara-ya svāhā*. Having recited this mantra, [one should proceed].
With both index fingers held upright like vajras,
this forms the Vajra Wall mudrā.
With both index fingers joined like a ring, this forms the Vajra Net mudrā.
In this manner, join the index fingers together;
this constitutes the Vajrakīla mudrā.
These three mudrās are to be used in conjunction with the mantra of the deity Ratnagarbha.
One obtains great protection.
Next, one invites the worthy sages and holy ones,
and constructs a fragrant altar before them.
Prepare incense candles using worm-free *gośīrṣa* sandalwood, aloeswood, and other such materials.
Holding these incense candles, face toward the worthy sages and saints;
with palms joined in reverence, keep the body steady and motionless.
Then recite this mantra:
*Ehi ehi svāgataṃ*. Having recited this mantra, form the mudrā of invocation by bending the thumb into the space between the index fingers.
Again, recite the mantra of invocation:
*Ratnapālanatekṣe he julu julu dhara dhara jarāṃśaya nabhriya rāya svāhā*. Recite the mantra of invocation.
Having already obtained the descent of the noble ones,
one should immediately join the palms and bend the third joints of each of the three fingers,
with the middle fingers placed side by side.
With the thumbs separated,
form the Lion Throne mudrā of the Treasure God (Ratnapāṇi) to offer as a seat;
this mudrā is formed by joining the middle fingers.
The deity Ratnapāla and his retinue all sit within it and make aspirations for the bestowal of gifts;
next, perform the rite of consecration.
Fashion a whisk from *uśīra* wood and paint the forms and colors of the honored deity and the sages thereon. Then,
form a fist with the right hand and place the left hand upon the waist.
Perform the action by using the *vīci-mudrā* to sweep away [impurities].
Recite the *viśuddhi-mantra* seven times and offer it to the worthy ones and the sages.
The mantra is as follows:
*Ratnapālanāte hara hara rājuga ra haranaya svāhā.* Furthermore, the ritual rules for binding and purifying the maṇḍala are explained.
Using *kūrmāsa* and incense to make a paste,
smear it upon the ground of the maṇḍala,
making each of the four sides twelve finger-widths wide.
If it is twelve finger-widths or more, it likewise accords with the ritual rules;
one then forms the seal of purification (*viśuddhi-mudrā*).
This is done by extending all five fingers of both hands.
Pointing the fingers away from one another and pressing them down against the ground,
once the seal of purification has been formed,
recite the maṇḍala mantra seven times.
The mantra is:
*tathāgatapradīpanate kuru kuru vārida pūraya svāhā*. Furthermore, the ritual procedure for offering lamps is explained.
Place yellow cow ghee in a new vessel and use cotton from a *tūla* tree as the wick for a lamp; then,
with both hands, form fists and join them together.
Extend the two thumbs and the two little fingers,
joining them together like a needle to form the *Ratnagarbha-dīpa-mudrā*.
Then, recite the Dīpa-mantra seven times.
The mantra is:
*Ratnapālanāthe hulu hulu prakarṣaya svāhā*. Furthermore, the ritual procedure for bathing the noble deities is explained.
If the image is made of gold, silver, jade, or stone,
one may bathe the body of the image with water;
if it is a clay塑 (plastic) image, a painted image, or a banner-image, [one should proceed accordingly].
One may bathe the reflected image by looking at it in a mirror,
or one may bathe the shadow of the image by facing the moon after nightfall,
saying these words: "I now offer this bath."
Then, join the two hands in *añjali* and interlace the two little fingers.
Pass the two ring fingers over them so that they enter into the palms.
Bring the tips of the two index fingers together and bend them into the shape of a ring.
Bend the upper joints of both thumbs;
this is the mudrā for bathing.
Then recite the bathing mantra seven times.
The mantra is:
*Ratnapātranate sattvān abhiryakhaṭa khaṭa paryāraṅkopa yaraḥ svāhā*. Furthermore, the ritual procedure for incense is explained.
Using incense free of insects, such as white sandalwood and gośīrṣa sandalwood, as an unguent, one forms the incense mudrā and speaks these words: "I now offer this incense.
Then, with both hands, the thumbs are brought toward each other.
Spread the two index fingers apart and bend them at the middle joints;
this forms the *vilepana-mudrā*.
Then recite the *vilepana-mantra* seven times.
The mantra is:
*Tat-tva-pa-ra-nan-te ra-ra-ra-ka-ra-ka-ra-su-gan-dha-gan-dhe pri-ye svā-hā*. Furthermore, the ritual procedure for burning incense is explained.
When filling and burning the incense burner with worm-free white sandalwood, gośīrṣa sandalwood,
aloeswood, olibanum, and so forth,
one should speak these words: "I now offer this incense."
With the tips of the thumbs of both hands,
press against the tips of the nails of the three fingers beginning with the middle finger,
and cause the two index fingers to bend at their third joints.
Form the incense-offering mudrā and again recite the incense-offering mantra seven times.
The mantra is as follows:
*Ratnapālanate dhrudhru mahādbhavapriyāya svāhā.* Furthermore, the ritual procedure for offering flowers is explained.
Jāti flowers, mālatī flowers,
mandārava flowers, lotus flowers,
utpala flowers, and māgura flowers, and so forth.
When making the offering,
one should say, "I now present these flowers," and simultaneously join the two fists facing each other with the fingers extended upward.
Extend the two thumbs to form the *puṣpāñjali* (flower-offering) mudrā.
Then recite the Flower-Offering Mantra seven times.
The mantra is as follows:
*Ratnapātranati puṣpa praruhi rihi puṣpa nigasa svāhā.* Furthermore, the ritual procedure for offering food at a mandala using five-colored powders is explained.
Using powders of five colors— blue, yellow, red, white, and green—
and having perfumed them with *jāti* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, and so forth,
one should single-mindedly draw the maṇḍala with these powders.
When making the food offering, one should speak these words: "I now offer this food.
Then, with both hands and all five fingers held level and upright, press them against the ground to form a mandala of five-colored powder;
this is the mudrā for the food offering.
Furthermore, recite the mantra for offering food at the five-colored powder mandala seven times.
The mantra is as follows:
*Tat-tva-pa-ra-na-te-he-he-ma-hā-pi-na-m-re-bri-ya-śu-pa-ya-svā-hā*. As for the food and drink that is offered:
Using high-quality granulated sugar, milk, and honey,
prepare various kinds of food and drink, as well as various kinds of ghee-based foods;
these include ghee, curd, rock sugar, and honey.
It is called the "Sweet Food of Samādhi," the most supreme among all foods;
it consists of the five grains, milk, vegetables, and so forth, endowed with every flavor.
One should make the offering during the day and conclude it during the night.
Furthermore, prepare yakṣa food complete with the three ingredients of ginger, salt, and black pepper;
offer this every night at the time of departure, but cease doing so during the day.
The practitioner who maintains the recitation must first beg for food—
such as milk, vegetables, or fruits—
and after having completed the fast with these meals, they shall purify themselves by bathing the body.
Nevertheless, one should practice and train in the dharmas one maintains,
ensuring they are mastered with proficiency;
[one should do so] using the three kinds of pure food and the like.
Outside the hall of the noble ones, beneath a great tree, he made an offering and spoke these words: "I now offer this food.
He then extended both hands flatly.
With the ten fingers straightened,
place the two thumbs within the palms to form the *bali-mudrā* (offering-food seal).
Then, recite the *bali-mantra* seven times.
The mantra is:
*tadna bāvanate śakāśakāmale rāja rānu kampa male dayakāne he he svāhā*. Furthermore, the ritual procedure for the bell is explained.
One must use a new bell containing a resonant tongue that produces the most exquisite sound;
it should be hung above the gateway of the maṇḍala while reciting these words: "I now offer this bell."
Immediately cover it downward with the right hand to form the bell mudrā.
Then recite the mantra for offering the bell seven times.
The mantra is as follows:
*Ratnaprabhānate kṣiṇi kṣiṇi gaṇṭhakaraṇa kuñci śrīṇani svāhā.* Furthermore, the ritual procedure for making a parasol is explained.
Construct the body with wood; use fresh,
clean white silk or similar materials for the hanging bands,
and paint figures of sages and deities upon these bands.
And having adorned the middle of the band with jewels to form a precious canopy,
one should speak these words: "I now offer this precious canopy."
Then, joining the palms and prostrating with the head,
one should form the *ratnacchatra-mudrā* by bending the middle sections of both hands so that they resemble a parasol.
Furthermore, one should recite the *Ratnacchatra-mantra* seven times.
The mantra is:
*Ratnapālanate gṛhṇa gṛhṇa caṭara piśu caṭara rākṣasa svāhā*. Furthermore, the ritual procedures for banners and streamers are explained.
The banners and streamers to be fashioned should be of fresh colors.
Then, with the left hand, press the thumb against the middle, ring, and little fingers;
extend the index finger upright and slightly tilted to form the mudrā of the banner.
With the thumb of the right hand, press the ring finger and the little finger;
extend the middle finger and the index finger upright,
and slightly tilt them while shaking them to form the Banner Mudrā (*dhvajamudrā*).
Furthermore, recite the mantra for offering the banner and pennant seven times.
The mantra is as follows:
*Tat-pā-dra-nā-de-ja-ya ja-ya tu-ru tu-ru ve-ja-yan-te pi-rya-svā-hā*. These are the twenty kinds of offerings.
The root mantra, the inner heart-seal, and the outer heart-seal may all be used interchangeably for empowerment and offerings.
Furthermore, form fists with both hands, with the little fingers extended like needles.
Form the mudrā of the Treasure Store Deity (*Ratnagarbha*).
Upon seeing this mudrā, the Treasure Store Deity within it becomes joyful.
I shall now explain the maṇḍala of that noble Treasure Store Deity.
It enables those who possess no wealth to obtain all riches, and those who lack virtue to acquire all goodness.
It can accomplish all undertakings, extinguish all transgressions,
and secure the prosperity and nobility of yakṣas.
Furthermore, having attained cohabitation with yakṣas,
he again taught the maṇḍala named Yakṣamukha.
In a pure, uninhabited land within a grove of trees,
one should smear the ground with cow dung and constantly make offerings of various fragrant flowers.
Recite the yakṣa mantra to perform the consecration rite;
recite the yakṣa heart-mantra to perform the invocation rite;
and construct the powder mandala according to the ritual rules.
That maṇḍala should be made square,
with one gate opening in each direction,
its orientation perfectly aligned.
In the center of the maṇḍala, one should place the deity Ratnagarbha,
seated upon a jewel-treasury,
adorned according to the prescribed sequence.
The color of his body is white, yellow, and red;
he further manifests as Śaṅkhagarbha and Padmagarbha;
on the left are Ratnagarbha and Amitābha.
The one on the right is named Ratnagarbha-kanakaprabha;
the yakṣa king is stationed in the east;
and in the southeast corner is the one named Maṇiprabha.
In the south is named Ratnaprabhā;
in the southwest corner is named Jalaprabhā;
in the west is named Nīlakaṇṭha.
The northwest corner is named Īśāna;
the north is named Ratnapāṇi.
These eight are the retinues of the Great Treasure Store Spirits.
If one seeks accomplishment within this root mantra,
one should contemplate it with a subtle mind and practice according to the Dharma.
If one does not rely upon it, it will be like laboring in vain upon the great earth.
This would cause those seekers to instead create demonic obstacles.
Therefore, with single-minded devotion, one should contemplate according to the ritual rules within the eight attendant positions of the maṇḍala,
aspiring for the attainment of siddhi.
All five heinous crimes shall be completely eradicated.
Furthermore, the practitioner must first observe the precepts of fasting and purity,
constantly practicing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
For the maṇḍala to be constructed, first prepare a clay platform that is level and square on all four sides;
sprinkle it with scented water for purification.
Then, move the powerful deity Ratnagarbha and install him in the northeast.
Then, in the center of the maṇḍala, one installs the principal deity, Śākyamuni Buddha.
He sits in the full lotus posture with eyes closed in the manner of one entering meditative absorption.
As the teacher of the three realms, his body is of true golden color and his uṣṇīṣa is perfectly complete.
The splendor of all adornments is supreme.
To the left of that Buddha resides the Great Radiant Bodhisattva named Ganges-Sand Fearless Avalokiteśvara.
The body possesses four arms and is colored like a swan;
it is like a *kumuda* flower, like the moon,
like a pearl, and like the color of milk.
Seated upon a lotus throne and holding a lotus in his hand,
his head is bound in a topknot and crowned with a celestial tiara;
above him is the Buddha Amitābha, whose auspicious marks are perfectly complete.
The reciter speaks these words: "I now offer this fly-whisk.
He then presses the thumb against the nail of the little finger with his right hand, while the remaining three fingers are held in the shape of a vajra.
Turning upward, perform the *vajrāveśa-mudrā* (the whisk-offering gesture).
Then, recite the *vajrāveśa-mantra* seven times.
The mantra is as follows:
*Ratnapātranati kṣama ra kṣama ra paryāya dhuṭa dhuṭa svāhā.* Furthermore, the ritual rules for adorning the Buddha’s body are explained.
The crowns, jeweled girdles, necklaces, and so forth that they wear are all adorned with gold and precious gems;
if gold and jewels were lacking, one would instead fashion these ornaments from wood.
Furthermore, using pigments such as orpiment to paint and adorn garments,
one should say: "I now offer this adornment," and immediately touch the two thumbs with both hands.
Press down on the lower three fingernails of the middle fingers with both hands;
hook the tips of the two index fingers together and turn them upward to form the Adornment Seal (*alaṃkāra-mudrā*).
Furthermore, recite the Adornment Mantra seven times. The mantra is:
*Tathāgatapadranādimigavaraṇajvalamukhana svāhā*. Next, the ritual rules for making offerings are explained.
With exquisite flower garlands, fragrant flowers, precious objects,
as well as arghya water, incense, medicinal herbs, pure garments, eye salve, golden chopsticks,
and arghya bowls containing a mixture of the five grains.
Making offerings to the noble ones, one speaks these words:
"I now present this argha offering before the lion throne."
Then, spread the thumb open to form the *argha* mudrā.
Recite the *argha* mantra seven times;
the mantra is to be recited as before.
Thus, the practitioner who maintains this recitation must first achieve mastery in the vidyā-mantra methods of the argha offering;
only then may they accomplish the argha offering by fashioning ten balls of food from crystal or other precious gems.
If one lacks the requisite conditions,
one may prepare ten morsels of food from five types of grain, such as mung beans;
this applies if one lacks the five grains.
One should then take the pure earth and form it into ten morsels of food as an offering.
Next, one should use fruits,
such as the *vījapūra* fruit and others.
One should offer as an offering auspicious and sweet fruits that have fallen naturally due to their exquisite fragrance and flavor, along with their leaves.
Next, use incense.
If exquisite incense is unavailable,
simply use the bark and flowers of fragrant trees, ground into powder.
Prepare incense and candles for offering;
next, use ghee lamps. If no ghee oil is available, [use an alternative].
One may use śrīśa wood, pine resin,
or similar substances to light lamps as an offering. If powdering the mandala,
one should use powdered fragments of the seven precious gems.
If the necessary conditions are lacking, one should use the flour of five-colored rice or wheat.
If rice or wheat flour is unavailable,
one may use white clay, stone powder, or clean sand.
Dye it into five colors so that it may be used as powder for the altar.
Next, prepare food offerings for the worthy ones and sages;
if there is no food or drink available, substitute them with fruits, medicinal roots, and the like.
According to these ritual procedures,
even if the reciter lacks certain conditions, they must provide twenty kinds of offerings.
This applies whether one is constructing a maṇḍala or not.
One must rely upon the practice of the ten pāramitās;
those who are free from sinful karma will achieve accomplishment.
Before long, they will swiftly attain the purity of the Dharma-eye and realize the fruit of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
If the aforementioned ten morsels of food are made from the five jewels, the five metals, or the five grains,
and if the morsels of food are made from the five grains:
It must be dyed to produce the colors of the five precious gems;
for instance, if mung beans are used as food,
they are dyed green.
Having fashioned [the offerings] from great blue gems and the like,
the reciter speaks these words:
"I now offer this argha and other offerings."
Next, the ritual procedure for dismissal is explained.
Use white sandalwood free of insects, gośīrṣa-candana, agallochum, nāgakeśara, and so forth.
Then, join the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb together.
Recite the mantra for dismissal seven times to consecrate [the offerings],
and then recite it three times.
All the invited worthy ones and sages shall each return to their original places according to their respective directions.
One should cast the fragrant parched rice toward the sky.
Using the *ākarṣaṇa-mudrā* (invocation seal), one spreads the fingers apart to form the *visarjana-mudrā* (dismissal seal).
The mantra for dismissal is as follows:
*Ratnapālanate hihikṛte dīptavajraprabhāṅgaścaśca svāhā*. The reciter then addresses himself as follows:
Out of my sincere faith, I act for your benefit;
I pray that you will graciously accept this arghya, incense, flowers, and so forth,
and together with your retinue, travel by way of the void.
They go to their original world, the supreme abode where the Fire Deity and other celestial beings dwell,
as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Devagarbha Sūtra*, and other such texts.
In this manner, there are noble ones and sages in each of the directions.
Fifty worlds away from here in the eastern direction, there is a world named Flower-Blossoming.
Therein dwells a World-Honored One named Flower-Blossoming King Tathāgata.
There dwells a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī. To the west,
there is a land called Sukhāvatī.
There resides a Blessed One named the Tathāgata Amitābha,
and there dwells a bodhisattva named Avalokiteśvara.
In the north there is a land named Aṇavatī.
There dwell the noble Bodhisattvas Vajrapāṇi, Ratnabhadra,
Pūrṇabhadra, the deity Vasudhara, and other great Bodhisattvas.
And he dwells therein.
Having thus restored these various assemblies to their original positions,
[he places] all the banners, streamers, and precious canopies within the front maṇḍala.
One should wish to offer incense, flowers, lamps, candles, staffs, whisks,
food, drink, and various exquisite substances such as arghya water and flowers.
At that time, the reciter stands before the right side of the noble deities;
he performs the offerings and the recitation from the left side.
Furthermore, those who participate in the ritual must first bathe and purify themselves according to the prescribed rules.
Once the invocation of the worthy sages and the offerings have been completed,
they should then be sent forth.
The Sūtra on the Ritual Manual of the Holy Treasure-God (Ārya-Mañjuśrī-māṇibhadra-dhāraṇī-vidhi-sūtra), Volume Upper;

Furthermore, regarding the articles for offering used within the maṇḍala,
twenty items must be prepared.
Offerings are presented three times each day.
Once the offerings have been made at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), they may not be used again at the hour of the Horse (11 a.m.–1 p.m. or the hour of the Rooster (5–7 p.m.).
One must replace it with a new one. However,
if the reciter lacks the means to do so,
it is permitted to pay its value and redeem it.
At the second and third sessions, offer the offerings once again;
do this at all three sessions every day until you have obtained the ritual for the maṇḍala.
On the day the sought-after accomplishment is achieved,
quickly pay the aforementioned full value of the price.
When making the offering:
Then, having bound the Banner Mudrā, recite the Banner Mantra as follows:
*Ratnapradīpanateḥ svākara-sattvārja-pūjaka svāhā*. Furthermore, the ritual rules for garments and articles are explained.
One should fashion two pairs of white garments made of silk free of insects, and upon the garments, paint the form of a stūpa adorned with gold-colored pigments.
Then, one should speak these words: "I now offer these articles of clothing."
Then, with both thumbs, each grasp the index finger and bend it into a ring;
hook the two rings together and splay the remaining fingers apart to form the *vastra-mudrā* (garment seal).
Furthermore, recite the mantra for clothing and articles seven times. The mantra is:
*Ratna-pratītya-dhiti dhiti mahā-samudra-mārutasvāhā*. Next, the ritual procedure for the fan is explained.
Use insect-free silk to make the fans.
The fans shall be white in color and their dimensions shall accord with the ritual regulations.
The handles must be straight and adorned at both ends with gold and precious gems.
Speaking these words, "I now offer this fan," one should immediately bend the little finger of the left hand into the palm, extend the arm,
and move the hand to form the *vījana-mudrā* (the fan seal).
Furthermore, recite the *śaṅkha* mantra seven times. The mantra is as follows:
*Ratnapātranati vai raṃ bhava yodhara kākarasa svāhā*. Next, the ritual procedure for waving the whisk (*cāmara*) is explained.
Fashion a white fly-whisk according to the ritual rules and decorate its handle with paintings.
Empower it by reciting the whisk mantra seven times.
Then, install the yakṣa king Nābha in the northeast.
In the north, one should place Vaiśravaṇa; in the northwest, Mahānābha;
and next, the Great Yakṣa King Aruṇīśvara.
Next, one should place *bhaṇmanahūnu hūnuka*,
as well as *sūkṣma-janava-jaṃbhakumudakara-kṛta ima-ma-hunadra*.
Next, place the yakṣiṇī Vairocanī;
this yakṣiṇī is most supremely beautiful.
Next, place Vairūpā.
Vāmaṇḍalin sūmahi mahi gavañca.
Svāhā jvala-jvala padma-sara.
Sphuruvaviñcā yakṣiṇī.
Mahāmāyāsūkṣmajaḥ (or Mahāmāyāsūkṣmajā)
vaṇamālācchavīśvarī
Naroma-mārikāja sarvaka-ma-phala-praṇa.
And *manujavakāmaruci-srutavākya-snigdha-nirjhariṇī*.
The twenty [mantras] beginning with *Mahāgārjite vikhyāta* and so forth,
or one hundred, should be installed in sequence in the outer directions.
Before the noble deities such as Indra,
one should manifest the vajra-net, wheel, spear, staff, conch, noose, banner, and trident; furthermore,
at the eastern gate, one should establish the trident, vajra-flames, and so forth.
In this manner, one may prepare more than a hundred varieties;
using *mālātī* flowers and *mallikā* flowers,
one should steep five-colored powders.
Offer powdered incense and burn aloeswood incense.
Reciting the Heart Mantra, invoke the Treasure-Store Deity (Vasudhara) and all the sages and holy ones.
Reciting the Root Mantra, invoke the yakṣiṇī.
Next, offer flower garlands, mālatī flowers,
exquisite lotuses, utpala flowers, kahlāra flowers,
kuruṇḍaka flowers, and kiṃśuka flowers.
Offer to all the worthy and noble ones in their proper sequence.
Perform homa with purple lac, guggulu incense, camphor,
and white sandalwood before the noble ones of the Treasure Repository.
Arrange various flowers and various articles of offering.
If one hears a great, evil sound as if something were being destroyed, this is an auspicious omen;
one must not be terrified.
The sought-after objective will be definitively accomplished;
one shall obtain a treasure-store deity and great wealth and nobility.
This is the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala.
And the mantra to be recited:
Oṃ jvālā-jvalana-ya svāhā | Adhipati-mahāyakṣa-rājādhipate yakṣa-pramardana yakṣa-savitre oṃ kṣa svāhā. Next is the heart-mantra.
Ānandabhadraya svāhā | Yakṣavidye svāhā. Next is the Lotus Treasury Mantra.
Araṇtaśaṅkhāya svāhā. Next, the mantra of Śaṅkhaśila:
Rājatanābhadhanadhipataye svāhā. Sonanābhadhanadhipataye svāhā.
maṇinābhaya dhanadipataye svāhā | ratnanābhaya dhanadipataye svāhā | sunābhaya dhanadipataye svāhā ||
Oṃ amr̥todbhavāya dharaṇīdharāyai svāhā | Oṃ nīrājanodbhavāya dharaṇīdharāyai svāhā | Oṃ vaiśramaṇāya dharaṇīdharāyai svāhā ||
mahānābaya dhanañjayāya svāhā | hara hara jagatpaka hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | jagatpakaya kṣaṇadraye svāhā ||
Hulu huluṇāṃ suṣṇāya svāhā | Hara hara caṇḍasiṃhāya svāhā | Jambhanāya svāhā ||
Mahānārayaṇāya svāhā | Vimara vimara nariṣaṇi svāhā | Vimara vimale viśrāṇaya nirghātaya svāhā | Caṇḍālaṃ śūmaniṣpīḍite niṣpīḍite caṇḍāle caṇḍāramade svāhā ||
Jālandharaśodhani svāhā | Avahani suluñcanīyapadme svāhā | Padmasarasorubhamanurame svāhā ||
Sphuru sphuru vāhu-pratāye svāhā | Vahivimale pracimuñca svāhā | Mahāmikha-sukṣma-le sukṣma-le kṣa-varaṇi svāhā.
Namaḥ āleṇi svāhā | Oṃ tiṣṭha puṣpale svāhā | Narmamale kaphale narmakile kile svāhā | Kamamale viraseṇi svāhā | Sarvagrahamanujāmukhavati svāhā | Kamarucivini svāhā | Surudavajyaṅkari svāhā ||
Svāhā to Sūnṛśāṅgi; svāhā to Mahoragaparyaṅki; svāhā to Indrāya niveditabhatte.
Oṃ agnayehavyavāhāya svāhā. Oṃ yamāya pṛthivīdharāya svāhā. These are the mantras.
It causes all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhūtas, piśācas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, to pay respect, offer praise, and experience great joy.
Furthermore, this mantra benefits all sentient beings like a wish-fulfilling gem, like that auspicious vase, and like that kalpavṛkṣa tree;
whatever is sought shall be accomplished.
I now proclaim this mantra-dharma for them to recite;
if sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness should even briefly hear this dharma,
those persons shall never again fall into the perils of the evil realms.
If there are sentient beings who have planted roots of goodness,
and who delight in hearing, copying, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [this],
the merit they obtain will be no different from that of a Buddha-Tathāgata.
If there is anyone who receives and upholds this heart-mantra,
that person shall enter the stage of non-retrogression and before long shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They will forever be free from the evil realms.
Such persons shall not be poor, nor old; they shall be without illness and without suffering, and all various matters shall be perfectly fulfilled for them.
Furthermore, one will attain the affection, respect, reverence, and offerings of all sentient beings.
I shall now briefly describe the merits obtained by upholding this mantra.
Even if all the worthy sages, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and so forth...
One cannot know the measure of this merit;
it cannot be fully described.
Thus it is for us and those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Even the Tathāgata could not exhaustively describe the merits of this mantra,
let alone a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or any among the devas and humans—
how could they know the measure of these merits and describe them in their entirety?
The merit of the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom is boundless;
the merit possessed by this powerful treasure-guardian spirit is likewise so.
This king of mantras is the true heart of all Tathāgatas;
it is able to act as the sovereign of all worlds and to save sentient beings who harbor evil intentions.
One who subdues the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings is able to give rise to all wisdom;
if one seeks the deity of the treasure storehouse, [one should look to such a person].
To the right of the Tathāgata, one should paint a divine image.
It is white in color, holding a fly-whisk in its hand, and its physical characteristics are perfectly complete.
To the right of this divine image, one should paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
He has the color of a blue utpala flower;
his physical form is adorned with pearls and is perfectly complete.
In front of the Bodhisattva, one should paint the yakṣa Mahākāruṇika Ratnasena.
His body is like the color of clear water and his physical marks are perfectly complete.
His face bears a gracious expression, and he holds a *vibhītaka* fruit in his hand.
He wears yellow garments and a large, tattered crown, and sits with his left leg extended.
In this manner, the reciter observes from head to foot,
ensuring that each detail of the ritual procedure is complete;
thus they maintain correct visualization for one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣa*).
Raising the mind, perform the visualization practice of making special offerings.
Imagine all the flowers produced in the water,
as well as the various beautiful fragrances of flowers on dry land.
By offering all kinds of precious jewels, exquisite garments,
as well as food, drink, lamps, flower garlands, and so forth,
one shall attain the fulfillment of all aspirations.
Having thus visualized with single-minded concentration,
the reciter further declares:
"In accordance with the ritual procedures of the Triple Gem, I accept and practice this with faith."
Thereafter, following the ritual procedures for devas and nāgas, perform the homa rite.
Visualize the Great General Ratnapāla grasping fire and bringing it to place within the homa hearth.
The Great General Pūrṇabhadra kindles the fire in the hearth;
the Great General Vasudhara performs the rite of purification;
and the Great General Vaiśravaṇa spreads the seat of auspicious kuśa grass.
One accomplishes the visualization according to the ritual procedures of the Tathāgata.
Next, one visualizes the head-mantra as kindling the fire and recites the mouth-mantra for the invocation.
Performing protection with the foot-mantra and seeking accomplishment,
one performs the homa until it is complete,
then casts [the offerings] three times by hand.
Recite the mantra:
*āgneye svāhā*. Then, form the auspicious mudrās and others:
join the two hands in the añjali gesture.
Place the noble ones in the center;
visualize them and recite the mantra for a brief moment, like fire fanned by the wind.

Visualize the aforementioned milk and perform one hundred thousand *homa* offerings; first offer one hundred thousand *homa* to the eight Great Vidyārājas, and next offer them to the Great Vidyārāja Ratnaśrī.
By performing one hundred thousand homas separately, one attains great wealth and status;
by two hundred thousand, one’s descendants will flourish;
and by three hundred thousand, even those who have committed great offenses [will be purified].
One shall also attain the methods for accomplishment.
Following these ritual procedures, one should perform them constantly with single-minded devotion.
Next, one performs the homa with water.
Soak flowers in water and perform one thousand *homa* offerings with scented water to the deity Ratnagarbha.
This will ensure that you constantly obtain wealth and perpetually experience happiness.
Furthermore, by performing one thousand *homa* offerings, one attains the method of increase (*puṣṭi*).
Following these ritual procedures,
perform the *homa* while visualizing as previously described until it is complete.
By offering three handfuls of water, one’s household will increase.
If one performs five hundred thousand *homa* offerings,
one can cause the painted image to conceal itself and cause hidden treasures (*nidhi*) to appear.
One shall enjoy inexhaustible resources and attain supreme bliss.
Furthermore, by performing the foot-mantra, the mouth-mantra,
and so forth, all things sought shall be accomplished.
One is able to restrain enemies, transcend the realm of Māra, and forever leave behind profound suffering.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, the merit one receives is equal to that of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Such is this Dharma.
The Sūtra on the Ritual Manual of the Noble Treasure God Ratnapāla, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume II.
